column1: # assets/traits.tsv: the traits panel of step 42 (docs/42-traits.md).
# Hand-curated from the primary papers in the pmids column; no text is taken from SNPedia or any
# other database. GRCh38; ref is the GRCh38 base, alt the allele the readings are about.
# hom_ref, het, hom_alt: the reading for ref/ref, ref/alt and alt/alt. ancestry: yes when the
# reading depends on ancestry (the note says how). tests/test_traits_table.py checks the schema.

column9: het

column7: Lactase persistence (digesting milk sugar as an adult)
column8: No copy of -13910T, the European lactase persistence allele: lactase activity usually falls after childhood, unless another row below carries a persistence allele.
column9: One copy of -13910T: lactase activity usually stays into adulthood.
column10: Two copies of -13910T: lactase activity usually stays into adulthood.
column12: Lactase persistence is dominant: one persistence allele at any of the five lactase rows is usually enough. -13910T explains it in Europeans; in Africa other alleles do (rows -14010, -13915, -13907), so read the five rows together.

column7: Lactase persistence (digesting milk sugar as an adult)
column8: No copy of -22018A, which travels with the -13910T persistence allele in Europeans.
column9: One copy of -22018A; read it with row rs4988235, which predicts persistence better.
column10: Two copies of -22018A; read it with row rs4988235, which predicts persistence better.
column12: A weaker marker than -13910: it matched lactase non-persistence in 229 of 236 cases of the original study, -13910 in all of them. Lactase persistence is dominant: one persistence allele at any of the five lactase rows is usually enough. -13910T explains it in Europeans; in Africa other alleles do (rows -14010, -13915, -13907), so read the five rows together.

column12: Found in Tanzanian, Kenyan and Sudanese people; it raises the activity of the lactase promoter in cell assays. column8: No ALDH2*2: acetaldehyde from alcohol is cleared normally.
column9: One ALDH2*2 copy (Glu504Lys). The inactive form is dominant: flushing, a fast heartbeat and nausea after alcohol are likely.
column10: Two ALDH2*2 copies: almost no ALDH2 activity; alcohol causes strong flushing and sickness.
column12: ALDH2*2 is common in East Asian people; the study typed livers of Japanese people.

column8: Two copies of ADH1B*2 (His48), a fast form of alcohol dehydrogenase. In a study of Chinese men it was less common among people with alcoholism.
column9: One copy of ADH1B*2 (His48), a fast form of alcohol dehydrogenase.
column10: No ADH1B*2: the usual ADH1B*1 (Arg48) form.
column12: The reference genome carries ADH1B*2, so here a match to the reference is the less common genotype in Europeans and Africans. ADH1B*2 is common in East Asia. The study names the gene by its old name, ADH2.

column8: C/C: in smokers, caffeine was broken down more slowly than with A/A; in non-smokers the genotypes did not differ.
column9: One A allele: in smokers the caffeine breakdown was close to C/C; in non-smokers the genotypes did not differ.
column10: A/A, the high-inducibility genotype: in smokers caffeine was broken down faster; in non-smokers the genotypes did not differ.
column12: Tested in 185 non-smokers and 51 smokers of European descent.

column8: No copy of the T allele linked to drinking more coffee.
column9: One T copy: on average about 0.2 cups of coffee a day more among coffee drinkers.
column10: Two T copies: on average about 0.4 cups of coffee a day more among coffee drinkers.
column12: An average effect in coffee drinkers from Iceland, the Netherlands, Germany and the USA; it says little about one person.

column8: Two copies of the T allele, linked to slightly lower habitual caffeine intake.
column9: One T and one C allele.
column10: Two copies of the C allele, linked to slightly higher habitual caffeine intake.
column12: A meta-analysis of 47,341 people of European descent; a small average effect.

column8: Ala49 on both copies, the residue of the non-taster form (AVI).
column9: Pro49 on one copy and Ala49 on the other.
column10: Pro49 on both copies, the residue of the taster form (PAV).
column12: Bitter taste of PTC and PROP follows the haplotype of three sites (rs713598, rs1726866, rs10246939): PAV (Pro49, Ala262, Val296) is the taster form and AVI (Ala49, Val262, Ile296) the non-taster form. The three rows are read one by one; which alleles sit on the same copy is not known here.

column8: Wet earwax (538G on both copies).
column9: Wet earwax: one copy of 538G is enough.
column10: Dry earwax (538A on both copies).
column12: Dry earwax is most common in East Asia, highest in Chinese and Koreans; wet earwax is common elsewhere.

column7: Photic sneeze reflex (sneezing in bright light)
column8: C/C: 40% of people with this genotype in the study sneezed in bright light.
column9: C/T: 32% of people with this genotype in the study sneezed in bright light.
column10: T/T: 28% of people with this genotype in the study sneezed in bright light.
column12: One genome-wide study of self-reported traits in research participants of mostly European ancestry; a small effect.

column8: A/A: 74% of people with this genotype in the study could smell it.
column9: A/G: 71% of people with this genotype in the study could smell it.
column10: G/G: 57% of people with this genotype in the study could smell it.
column12: Self-reported in research participants of mostly European ancestry. A later study confirmed the olfactory receptor region on chromosome 1 with other markers.

column8: 577R on both copies: alpha-actinin-3 is made in fast-twitch muscle fibres.
column9: One 577X copy: alpha-actinin-3 is still made.
column10: 577X on both copies: no alpha-actinin-3 in fast-twitch fibres, as in about 18% of white people. It causes no disease; the 577R allele was more common in elite sprint athletes.
column12: The athletic effect was seen in elite athletes and is small for most people.

column8: Brown eyes are most likely.
column9: Brown eyes are more likely than blue.
column10: Blue or other light eyes are most likely.
column12: The G allele lowers OCA2 expression in the iris. Studied in people of European descent.

column8: No OCA2 419Q.
column9: One OCA2 419Q copy, which changes how strongly rs12913832 predicts eye colour.
column10: Two OCA2 419Q copies, which change how strongly rs12913832 predicts eye colour.
column12: A modifier of the rs12913832 reading, not an eye-colour call on its own.

column8: 374Leu on both copies: in people of European descent this genotype went with dark hair, skin and eyes.
column9: 374Leu on one copy and 374Phe on the other.
column10: 374Phe on both copies, the common form in Europeans: lighter hair, skin and eyes than with 374Leu.
column12: The allele frequencies differ strongly between populations; the association was measured in people of European descent.

column8: Thr111 on both copies, the form nearly fixed in Europeans; it goes with lighter skin.
column9: Thr111 on one copy and Ala111 on the other.
column10: Ala111 on both copies, the ancestral form common in African and East Asian populations.
column12: The reference genome carries Thr111. In admixed populations each Thr111 copy went with lighter skin.

column8: No copy of the T allele linked to freckles and sun-sensitive skin.
column9: One T copy: freckles, sun-sensitive skin and brown rather than blond hair are more likely.
column10: Two T copies: freckles, sun-sensitive skin and brown rather than blond hair are more likely.
column12: Studied in people of European ancestry, where the T allele is found.

column7: Red hair and fair skin (MC1R R151C)
column8: No R151C.
column9: One R151C copy, a red-hair variant of MC1R: fair skin that tans poorly is more likely.
column10: Two R151C copies: red hair and fair skin that tans poorly are likely.
column12: Red hair usually needs a red-hair MC1R variant on both copies of the gene: the same one twice, or two different ones (rows rs1805007, rs1805008, rs1805009). One copy at two of these rows can mean one on each copy; the phase is not known here. MC1R variants are necessary but not always sufficient for red hair.

column7: Red hair and fair skin (MC1R R160W)
column8: No R160W.
column9: One R160W copy, a red-hair variant of MC1R: fair skin that tans poorly is more likely.
column10: Two R160W copies: red hair and fair skin that tans poorly are likely.
column12: Red hair usually needs a red-hair MC1R variant on both copies of the gene: the same one twice, or two different ones (rows rs1805007, rs1805008, rs1805009). One copy at two of these rows can mean one on each copy; the phase is not known here. MC1R variants are necessary but not always sufficient for red hair.

column7: Red hair and fair skin (MC1R D294H)
column8: No D294H.
column9: One D294H copy, a red-hair variant of MC1R: fair skin that tans poorly is more likely.
column10: Two D294H copies: red hair and fair skin that tans poorly are likely.
column12: Red hair usually needs a red-hair MC1R variant on both copies of the gene: the same one twice, or two different ones (rows rs1805007, rs1805008, rs1805009). One copy at two of these rows can mean one on each copy; the phase is not known here. MC1R variants are necessary but not always sufficient for red hair.

column8: 370Val on both copies, the usual form outside East Asia.
column9: One 370Ala copy, which goes with thicker head hair.
column10: 370Ala on both copies: thicker head hair is likely.
column12: 370Ala arose in Asia after the split from Europeans and is common in East Asia; the study calls it Asian-specific.

column8: 677C on both copies: the usual MTHFR enzyme.
column9: One 677T copy: somewhat lower MTHFR activity and a heat-sensitive enzyme.
column10: 677T on both copies: lower MTHFR activity and, on average, higher blood homocysteine.
column12: Common (about 38% of chromosomes in the original study carry 677T). Studied as a possible vascular risk factor; it is not a diagnosis.

column8: Secretor: FUT2 works, and blood group antigens are in saliva and other body fluids.
column9: Secretor: one working FUT2 copy is enough.
column10: Non-secretor, as about 20% of people are: no blood group antigens in saliva. In a challenge study nobody with this genotype was infected by Norwalk virus.
column12: The stop codon is W143X in the original numbering. Other FUT2 variants, not in this table, can also make a person a non-secretor.

column8: No copy of the G allele linked to lower vitamin D.
column9: One G copy: on average lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
column10: Two G copies: on average the lowest 25-hydroxyvitamin D (in one cohort 64.6 against 82.6 nmol/L for T/T).
column12: A genome-wide study of 33,996 people of European descent; sun, diet and supplements matter more.

column8: No copy of the T allele.
column9: One T copy: a carrier; the Gilbert genotype needs two.
column10: Two T copies: the genotype of Gilbert syndrome (about 10% of UK Biobank participants), with higher bilirubin. Only 3% of people with it had the diagnosis recorded.
column12: A marker strongly associated with Gilbert syndrome, measured in people of European ancestry. Step 07 (PharmCAT) reports UGT1A1 for drugs.

column8: No CYP2A6*2 (Leu160His).
column9: One CYP2A6*2 copy: that copy makes an inactive enzyme.
column10: Two CYP2A6*2 copies: no CYP2A6 activity from these copies, so nicotine is cleared slowly.
column12: CYP2A6*2 is rare (1 to 3% in Finnish, Spanish and Swedish people). Other CYP2A6 alleles, deletions included, are not read here; step 32 (pypgx) calls CYP2A6 from the BAM.

column8: Cys112 on both copies: no e4 change.
column9: Arg112 on one copy, the change that defines e4.
column10: Arg112 on both copies, the change that defines e4.
column12: Read with the APOE line, which combines rs429358 and rs7412 into the e2, e3 and e4 alleles. e4 is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, not a diagnosis.

column9: Cys158 on one copy, the change that defines e2.
